The goal, as stated in the OP, is rather less than clear.

    """

A common way of writing a multi-line python expression is to use an "extra" pair of parentheses. If I knew how you were evaluating "correct behavior" then I could assess whether this proposed solution is a good fit for your (unstated) goal.

Q: Securely implementing two factor authentication in flask A: 
from flask import Blueprint, request, jsonify, session
from flask_limiter import Limiter
from flask_limiter.util import get_remote_address
import pyotp

# Assume limiter is initialized in your app
limiter = Limiter(key_func=get_remote_address)

@api.post("/admin/2fa/verify")
@limiter.limit("5 per minute")  # Prevents brute force
def verify_admin_2fa():
    # 1. Ensure the user is actually in the middle of a login flow
    # Don't take user_id from the JSON body; take it from a secure session
    user_id = session.get("pending_2fa_user_id")
    if not user_id:
        return jsonify({"error": "Session expired or invalid"}), 401

    data = request.get_json() or {}
    code = str(data.get("code", "")).strip()

    user = User.query.get(user_id)
    
    # Generic error to prevent account enumeration
    if not user or not user.is_admin or not user.two_fa or not user.two_fa.enabled:
        return jsonify({"error": "Authentication failed"}), 403

    secret = decrypt_secret(user.two_fa.encrypted_secret)
    totp = pyotp.TOTP(secret)

    # 2. Verify the code
    if totp.verify(code, valid_window=1):
        # 3. PREVENT REPLAY: Check if this time-step was already used
        current_otp_timecode = totp.timecode(totp.datetime.datetime.now())
        if user.two_fa.last_used_timecode >= current_otp_timecode:
            return jsonify({"error": "Code already used"}), 401

        # 4. Mark the code as used in the DB
        user.two_fa.last_used_timecode = current_otp_timecode
        db.session.commit()

        # 5. Finalize the login
        session["user_id"] = user.id
        session.pop("pending_2fa_user_id") 
        
        return jsonify({"status": "verified"})
    
    return jsonify({"error": "Invalid 2FA code"}), 401

Q: MySQL SQL STATE[HY000] [1203] User XXXXX already has more than 'max_user_connections' active connections A:

How to increase MySql connections Ref: https://ubiq.co/database-blog/how-to-increase-max-connections-in-mysql/

  1. Check the default max connections Log into MySQL command line tool and run the following command to get the current default max connections supported by your database server.

    mysql> show variables like "max_connections";

You will see the following output.

+-----------------+-------+
| Variable_name   | Value |
+-----------------+-------+
| max_connections | 100   |
+-----------------+-------+

Bonus Read : How to Change MySQL Timezone in Query

  1. Increase Max Connections There are two ways to increase MySQL connections. Here’s the command to update max connections to 200 via MySQL command line tool without restart.

    mysql> set global max_connections = 200;

The above command will increase max connections without restart but once the server is restarted, the changes will be gone. This method is useful to increase available connections in a production system such as a website/app, without having to restart your database server.

To permanently increase max connections, open my.cnf file,

$ sudo vi /etc/my.cnf

Depending on your Linux distribution and type of installation, my.cnf file may be located at any of the following locations.

/etc/my.cnf
/etc/mysql/my.cnf
$MYSQL_HOME/my.cnf
~/.my.cnf

Add the following line under [mysqld] section.

max_connections = 200

Now if you restart MySQL server, the changes will persist.

  1. Restart MySQL Server Restart MySQL Server to apply changes

    $ sudo service mysql restart
